[Contains English characters] Morality has three principal meanings.
[Contains English characters] In its first, descriptive usage, morality means a code of conduct or a set of beliefs distinguishing between right and wrong behaviors.
[Contains English characters] Descriptive morality does not explain why any behavior should be considered right or wrong, only that it may be classified so.
[Contains English characters] For the most part right and wrong acts are classified as such because they cause benefit or harm, respectively.
[Contains English characters] However, this is not by any means an all encompassing criterion.
[Contains English characters] It is possible that many moral beliefs are based on prejudice, ignorance or even hatred.
[Contains English characters] In its second, normative and universal sense, morality refers to an ideal code of belief and conduct which would be preferred by the sane moral person, under specified conditions.
[Contains English characters] In this definitive sense, claims are made such as Killing is immoral.
[Contains English characters] While descriptive morality would not necessarily disagree that killing is immoral, it would prefer to say, Many believe that killing is immoral.
[Contains English characters] A refined adherence to this latter position is known as moral skepticism, in which the unchanging existence of a rigid, universal, objective moral truth is rejected.
[Contains English characters] In its third usage, morality is synonymous with ethics.
[Contains English characters] Ethics is the systematic philosophical study of the moral domain.
[Contains English characters] Ethics seeks to address questions such as how a moral outcome can be achieved in a specific situation, how moral values should be determined, what morals people actually abide by, what the fundamental nature of ethics or morality is, including whether it has any objective justification, and how moral capacity or moral agency develops and what its nature is .
[Contains English characters] In applied ethics, for example, the prohibition against taking human life is controversial with respect to capital punishment, euthanasia, abortion and wars of invasion.
[Contains English characters] In normative ethics, a typical question might be whether a lie told for the sake of protecting someone from harm is justified.
[Contains English characters] In meta-ethics, a key issue is the meaning of the terms moral or immoral.
[Contains English characters] Moral realism would hold that there are true moral statements which report objective moral facts, whereas moral anti-realism would hold that morality is derived from any one of the norms prevalent in society ; the edicts of a god ; is merely an expression of the speakers sentiments ; an implied imperative ; or falsely presupposes that there are objective moral facts .
[Contains English characters] Some thinkers hold that there is no correct definition of right behavior, that morality can only be judged with respect to particular situations, within the standards of particular belief systems and socio-historical contexts.
[Contains English characters] This position, known as moral relativism, often cites empirical evidence from anthropology as evidence to support its claims.
[Contains English characters] The opposite view, that there are universal, eternal moral truths are known as moral absolutism.
[Contains English characters] Moral absolutists might concede that forces of social conformity significantly shape moral decisions, but deny that cultural norms and customs define morally right behavior.
[Contains English characters] Celia Green has made a distinction between tribal and territorial morality.
[Contains English characters] She characterizes the latter as predominantly negative and proscriptive: it defines a person’s territory, including his or her property and dependents, which is not to be damaged or interfered with.
[Contains English characters] Apart from these proscriptions, territorial morality is permissive, allowing the individual whatever behaviour does not interfere with the territory of another.
[Contains English characters] By contrast, tribal morality is prescriptive, imposing the norms of the collective on the individual.
[Contains English characters] These norms will be arbitrary, culturally dependent and ‘flexible’, whereas territorial morality aims at rules which are universal and absolute, such as Kant’s ‘categorical imperative’.
[Contains English characters] Green relates the development of territorial morality to the rise of the concept of private property, and the ascendancy of contract over status.
[Contains English characters] some observers hold that individuals apply distinct sets of moral rules to people depending on their membership of an ingroup or an outgroup .
[Contains English characters] Some biologists, anthropologists and evolutionary psychologists believe this ingroup-outgroup discrimination has evolved because it enhances group survival.
[Contains English characters] Gary R.
[Contains English characters] Johnson and V. S. Falger have argued that nationalism and patriotism are forms of this ingroup/outgroup boundary.
[Contains English characters] Jonathan Haidt has noted that experimental observation indicates an ingroup criterion provides one moral foundation substantially used by conservatives, but far less so by liberals.
[Contains English characters] Peterson and Seligman approach the anthropological view looking across cultures and across millennia.
[Contains English characters] They conclude that certain virtues have prevailed in all cultures they examined.
[Contains English characters] The major virtues they identified include wisdom / knowledge; courage; humanity; justice; temperance; and transcendence.
[Contains English characters] Each of these includes several divisions.
[Contains English characters] For instance humanity includes love, kindness, and social intelligence.
[Contains English characters] Fons Trompenaars, author of Did the Pedestrian Die?
[Contains English characters] , tested members of different cultures with various moral dilemmas.
[Contains English characters] One of these was whether the driver of a car would have his friend, a passenger riding in the car, lie in order to protect the driver from the consequences of driving too fast and hitting a pedestrian.
[Contains English characters] Trompenaars found that different cultures had quite different expectations .
[Contains English characters] The development of modern morality is a process closely tied to the Sociocultural evolution of humanity, however its roots are probably to be found in our very nature.
[Contains English characters] Some evolutionary biologists, particularly sociobiologists, believe that morality is a product of evolutionary forces acting at an individual level and also at the group level through group selection .
[Contains English characters] Some sociobiologists contend that the set of behaviors that constitute morality evolved largely because they provided possible survival and/or reproductive benefits .
[Contains English characters] Humans consequently evolved pro-social emotions, such as feelings of empathy or guilt, in response to these moral behaviors.
[Contains English characters] In this respect, morality is not absolute, but relative and constitutes any set of behaviors that encourage human cooperation based on their ideology.
[Contains English characters] Biologists contend that all social animals, from ants to elephants, have modified their behaviors, by restraining selfishness in order to make group living worthwhile.
[Contains English characters] Human morality, though sophisticated and complex relative to other animals, is essentially a natural phenomenon that evolved to restrict excessive individualism and foster human cooperation.
[Contains English characters] On this view, moral codes are ultimately founded on emotional instincts and intuitions that were selected for in the past because they aided survival and reproduction .
[Contains English characters] Examples: the maternal bond is selected for because it improves the survival of offspring; the Westermarck effect, where close proximity during early years reduces mutual sexual attraction, underpins taboos against incest because it decreases the likelihood of genetically risky behaviour such as inbreeding.
[Contains English characters] The phenomenon of reciprocity in nature is seen by evolutionary biologists as one way to begin to understand human morality.
[Contains English characters] Its function is typically to ensure a reliable supply of essential resources, especially for animals living in a habitat where food quantity or quality fluctuates unpredictably.
[Contains English characters] For example, some vampire bats fail to feed on prey on any given night while others consume a surplus.
[Contains English characters] Bats that have successfully fed then regurgitate part of their blood meal to save a conspecific from starvation.
[Contains English characters] Since these animals live in close-knit groups over many years, an individual can count on other group members to return the favor on nights when it goes hungry Marc Bekoff and Jessica Pierce have argued that morality is a suite of behavioral capacities likely shared by all mammals living in complex social groups .
[Contains English characters] They define morality as a suite of interrelated other-regarding behaviors that cultivate and regulate complex interactions within social groups.
[Contains English characters] This suite of behaviors includes empathy, reciprocity, altruism, cooperation, and a sense of fairness.
[Contains English characters] In related work, it has been convincingly demonstrated that chimpanzees show empathy for each other in a wide variety of contexts.
[Contains English characters] They also possess the ability to engage in deception, and a level of social politics prototypical of our own tendencies for gossip and reputation management.
[Contains English characters] Christopher Boehm has hypothesized that the incremental development of moral complexity throughout hominid evolution was due to the increasing need to avoid disputes and injuries in moving to open savanna and developing stone weapons.
[Contains English characters] Other theories are that increasing complexity was simply a correlate of increasing group size and brain size, and in particular the development of theory of mind abilities.
[Contains English characters] Richard Dawkins in The God Delusion suggested that our morality is a result of our biological evolutionary history and that the Moral Zeitgeist helps describe how morality evolves from biological and cultural origins and evolves with time within a culture.
[Contains English characters] Research on mirror neurons, since their discovery in 1996, suggests that they may have a role to play not only in action understanding, but also in emotion sharing empathy.
[Contains English characters] Cognitive neuro-scientist Jean Decety thinks that the ability to recognize and vicariously experience what another individual is undergoing was a key step forward in the evolution of social behavior, and ultimately, morality.
[Contains English characters] The inability to feel empathy is one of the defining characteristics of psychopathy, and this would appear to lend support to Decetys view.
[Contains English characters] The explicit making of moral right and wrong judgments links to activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex while as theintuitive reactions to situations containing implicit moral issues activates the temporoparietal junction area.
[Contains English characters] In modern moral psychology, morality is considered to change through personal development.
[Contains English characters] A number of psychologists have produced theories on the development of morals, usually going through stages of different morals.
[Contains English characters] Lawrence Kohlberg, Jean Piaget, and Elliot Turiel have cognitive-developmental approaches to moral development; to these theorists morality forms in a series of constructive stages or domains.
[Contains English characters] Social psychologists such as Martin Hoffman and Jonathan Haidt emphasize social and emotional development based on biology, such as empathy.
[Contains English characters] Moral identity theorists, such as William Damon and Mordechai Nisan, see moral commitment as arising from the development of a self-identity that is defined by moral purposes: this moral self-identity leads to a sense of responsibility to pursue such purposes.
[Contains English characters] Of historical interest in psychology are the theories of psychoanalysts such as Sigmund Freud, who believe that moral development is the product of aspects of the super-ego as guilt-shame avoidance.
[Contains English characters] If morality is the answer to the question how ought we to live at the individual level, politics can be seen as addressing the same question at the social level.
[Contains English characters] It is therefore unsurprising that evidence has been found of a relationship between attitudes in morality and politics.
[Contains English characters] Jonathan Haidt and Jesse Graham have studied the differences between liberals and conservatives, in this regard.
[Contains English characters] Haidt found that Americans who identified as liberals tended to value care and fairness higher than loyalty, respect and purity.
[Contains English characters] Self-identified conservative Americans valued care and fairness less and the remaining three values more.
[Contains English characters] Both groups gave care the highest over-all weighting, but conservatives valued fairness the lowest, whereas liberals valued purity the lowest.
[Contains English characters] Haidt also hypothesizes that the origin of this division in the United States can be traced to geohistorical factors, with conservatism strongest in closely knit, ethnically homogenous communities, in contrast to port-cities, where the cultural mix is greater, thus requiring more liberalism.
[Contains English characters] Group morality develops from shared concepts and beliefs and is often codified to regulate behavior within a culture or community.
[Contains English characters] Various defined actions come to be called moral or immoral.
[Contains English characters] Individuals who choose moral action are popularly held to possess moral fiber, whereas those who indulge in immoral behavior may be labeled as socially degenerate.
[Contains English characters] The continued existence of a group may depend on widespread conformity to codes of morality; an inability to adjust moral codes in response to new challenges is sometimes credited with the demise of a community .
[Contains English characters] Within nationalist movements, there has been some tendency to feel that a nation will not survive or prosper without acknowledging one common morality, regardless of in what it consists.
[Contains English characters] Political Morality is also relevant to the behaviour internationally of national governments, and to the support they receive from their host population.
[Contains English characters] Noam Chomsky states that Codified morality is generally distinguished from custom, another way for a community to define appropriate activity, by the formers derivation from natural or universal principles.
[Contains English characters] In certain religious communities, the Divine is said to provide these principles through revelation, sometimes in great detail.
[Contains English characters] Such codes may be called laws, as in the Law of Moses, or community morality may be defined through commentary on the texts of revelation, as in Islamic law.
[Contains English characters] Such codes are distinguished from legal or judicial right, including civil rights, which are based on the accumulated traditions, decrees and legislation of a political authority, though these latter often invoke the authority of the moral law.
[Contains English characters] Morality can also be seen as the collection of beliefs as to what constitutes a good life.
[Contains English characters] Since throughout most of human history, religions have provided both visions and regulations for an ideal life, morality is often confused with religious precepts.
[Contains English characters] In secular communities, lifestyle choices, which represent an individuals conception of the good life, are often discussed in terms of morality.
[Contains English characters] Individuals sometimes feel that making an appropriate lifestyle choice invokes a true morality, and that accepted codes of conduct within their chosen community are fundamentally moral, even when such codes deviate from more general social principles.
[Contains English characters] Moral codes are often complex definitions of moral and immoral that are based upon well-defined value systems.
[Contains English characters] Although some people might think that a moral code is simple, rarely is there anything simple about ones values, ethics, etc.
[Contains English characters] or, for that matter, the judgment of those of others.
[Contains English characters] The difficulty lies in the fact that morals are often part of a religion and more often than not about culture codes.
[Contains English characters] Sometimes, moral codes give way to legal codes, which couple penalties or corrective actions with particular practices.
[Contains English characters] Note that while many legal codes are merely built on a foundation of religious and/or cultural moral codes, oftentimes they are one and the same.
[Contains English characters] Examples of moral codes include the Golden Rule; the Five Precepts and the Noble Eightfold Path of Buddhism ; the ancient Egyptian code of Maat ;the ten commandments of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; the yamas and niyama of the Hindu scriptures; the ten Indian commandments; and the principle of the Dessek.
[Contains English characters] Another related concept is the moral core which is assumed to be innate in each individual, to those who accept that differences between individuals are more important than posited Creators or their rules.
[Contains English characters] This, in some religious systems and beliefs, is assumed to be the basis of all aesthetics and thus moral choice.
[Contains English characters] Moral codes as such are therefore seen as coercive—part of human politics.
[Contains English characters] In the scientific literature, the degree of religiosity is generally found to be associated with higher ethical attitudes.
[Contains English characters] Although a recent study by Gregory S.
[Contains English characters] Paul published in the Journal of Religion and Society argues for a positive correlation between the degree of public religiosity in a society and certain measures of dysfunction, an analysis published later in the same journal contends that a number of methodological problems undermine any findings or conclusions to be taken from the research.
[Contains English characters] In another response, Gary Jensen builds on and refines Pauls study.
[Contains English characters] His conclusion, after carrying out elaborate multivariate statistical studies, is that a complex relationship exists between religiosity and homicide with some dimensions of religiosity encouraging homicide and other dimensions discouraging it.
[Contains English characters] Meanwhile, other studies seem to show positive links in the relationship between religiosity and moral behavior—for example, surveys suggesting a positive connection between faith and altruism.
[Contains English characters] Modern research in criminology also acknowledges an inverse relationship between religion and crime, with many studies establishing this beneficial connection .
[Contains English characters] Indeed, a meta-analysis of 60 studies on religion and crime concluded, “religious behaviors and beliefs exert a moderate deterrent effect on individuals’ criminal behavior”.
[Contains English characters] Many religions provide moral guidelines for their followers.
[Contains English characters] They believe that God has instructed them with a way to live, and that following these rules will lead to oneness with God.

[Contains English characters] Also in the early 1900s, motion picture production companies from New York and New Jersey started moving to California because of the good weather and longer days.
[Contains English characters] Although electric lights existed at that time, none were powerful enough to adequately expose film; the best source of illumination for movie production was natural sunlight.
[Contains English characters] Besides the moderate, dry climate, they were also drawn to the state because of its open spaces and wide variety of natural scenery.
[Contains English characters] Another reason was the distance of Southern California from New Jersey, which made it more difficult for Thomas Edison to enforce his motion picture patents.
[Contains English characters] At the time, Edison owned almost all the patents relevant to motion picture production and, in the East, movie producers acting independently of Edisons Motion Picture Patents Company were often sued or enjoined by Edison and his agents.
[Contains English characters] Thus, movie makers working on the West Coast could work independently of Edisons control.
[Contains English characters] If he sent agents to California, word would usually reach Los Angeles before the agents did and the movie makers could escape to nearby Mexico.

[Contains English characters] होसन्नाची हाकIn The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, a hosanna shout is an organized ritual by a congregation of shouting hosanna.
[Contains English characters] It was first performed as a ritual in the dedication of the Kirtland Temple, and was a part of the Kirtland Endowment ceremony.
[Contains English characters] It continues to be practiced by some Latter Day Saint denominations, most notably The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, which practices the ritual at the dedication of each of its temples.
[Contains English characters] The sacred ceremony of the Hosanna Shout is practiced by members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.
[Contains English characters] It is usually reserved for temple dedications.
[Contains English characters] It is given in the spirit of thanksgiving and petition, fulfilling the instruction to bless the name of the Lord with loud voices and with a sound of rejoicing, with hosannas to him that sitteth upon the throne forever .
[Contains English characters] When the ordinance of the washing of feet was introduced at Kirtland, shouts of hosanna were viewed as a sealing benediction on both private and quorum prayer and then on the dedicatory prayer.
[Contains English characters] At prayer meetings in the Kirtland Temple, the Saints sometimes used related phrases such as Blessed is the name of the Most High God and Glory to God in the highest .
[Contains English characters] The Hosanna Shout is whole-souled, given to the full limit of ones strength.
[Contains English characters] The congregation stands and in unison shouts the words Hosanna, Hosanna, Hosanna to God and the Lamb.
[Contains English characters] Amen, Amen, and Amen, repeating the phrase three times.
[Contains English characters] This is done while waving of a white handkerchiefs with uplifted hands.
[Contains English characters] The epithet Lamb relates to the condescension and Atonement of Jesus Christ.
[Contains English characters] The Hosanna Shout memorializes the pre-earthly Council in Heaven, as when…all the sons of God shouted for joy .
[Contains English characters] It also recalls the hosannas and the waving of palm branches accorded the Messiah as he entered Jerusalem.
[Contains English characters] And hosannas welcomed him as he appeared to the Nephites.
[Contains English characters] President Lorenzo Snow, the fifth prophet of the restored church, taught that this shout will herald the Messiah when he comes in the glory of the Father .

[Contains English characters] An information resource is identified by a Uniform Resource Identifier and may be a web page, image, video, or other piece of content.
[Contains English characters] Hyperlinks present in resources enable users to easily navigate their browsers to related resources.
[Contains English characters] Although browsers are primarily intended to access the World Wide Web, they can also be used to access information provided by web servers in private networks or files in file systems.
[Contains English characters] The history of the web browser dates back to the late 1980s, when a variety of technologies laid the foundation for the first web browser, WorldWideWeb, by Tim Berners-Lee in 1991. That browser brought together a variety of existing and new software and hardware technologies.
[Contains English characters] The introduction of the NCSA Mosaic web browser in 1993 – one of the first graphical web browsers – led to an explosion in web use.
[Contains English characters] Marc Andreessen, the leader of the Mosaic team at NCSA, soon started his own company, named Netscape, and released the Mosaic-influenced Netscape Navigator in 1994, which quickly became the worlds most popular browser, accounting for 90% of all web use at its peak .

[Contains English characters] The primary purpose of a web browser is to bring information resources to the user.
[Contains English characters] This process begins when the user inputs a Uniform Resource Identifier, for example http://en. wikipedia. org/, into the browser.
[Contains English characters] The prefix of the URI determines how the URI will be interpreted.
[Contains English characters] The most commonly used kind of URI starts with http: and identifies a resource to be retrieved over the Hypertext Transfer Protocol .
[Contains English characters] Many browsers also support a variety of other prefixes, such as https: for HTTPS, ftp: for the File Transfer Protocol, and file: for local files.
[Contains English characters] Prefixes that the web browser cannot directly handle are often handed off to another application entirely.
[Contains English characters] For example, mailto: URIs are usually passed to the users default e-mail application, and news: URIs are passed to the users default newsgroup reader.
[Contains English characters] In the case of http, https, file, and others, once the resource has been retrieved the web browser will display it.
[Contains English characters] HTML is passed to the browsers layout engine to be transformed from markup to an interactive document.
[Contains English characters] Aside from HTML, web browsers can generally display any kind of content that can be part of a web page.
[Contains English characters] Most browsers can display images, audio, video, and XML files, and often have plug-ins to support Flash applications and Java applets.
[Contains English characters] Upon encountering a file of an unsupported type or a file that is set up to be downloaded rather than displayed, the browser prompts the user to save the file to disk.
[Contains English characters] Information resources may contain hyperlinks to other information resources.
[Contains English characters] Each link contains the URI of a resource to go to.
[Contains English characters] When a link is clicked, the browser navigates to the resource indicated by the links target URI, and the process of bringing content to the user begins again.
[Contains English characters] Available web browsers range in features from minimal, text-based user interfaces with bare-bones support for HTML to rich user interfaces supporting a wide variety of file formats and protocols.
[Contains English characters] Browsers which include additional components to support e-mail, Usenet news, and Internet Relay Chat, are sometimes referred to as Internet suites rather than merely web browsers.
[Contains English characters] All major web browsers allow the user to open multiple information resources at the same time, either in different browser windows or in different tabs of the same window.
[Contains English characters] Major browsers also include pop-up blockers to prevent unwanted windows from popping up without the users consent.
[Contains English characters] Most web browsers can display a list of web pages that the user has bookmarked so that the user can quickly return to them.
[Contains English characters] Bookmarks are also called Favorites in Internet Explorer.
[Contains English characters] In addition, all major web browsers have some form of built-in web feed aggregator.
[Contains English characters] In Mozilla Firefox, web feeds are formatted as live bookmarks and behave like a folder of bookmarks corresponding to recent entries in the feed.
[Contains English characters] In Opera, a more traditional feed reader is included which stores and displays the contents of the feed.
[Contains English characters] Furthermore, most browsers can be extended via plug-ins, downloadable components that provide additional features.
[Contains English characters] Most major web browsers have these user interface elements in common: Major browsers also possess incremental find features to search within a web page.
[Contains English characters] Most browsers support HTTP Secure and offer quick and easy ways to delete the web cache, cookies, and browsing history.
[Contains English characters] For a comparison of the current security vulnerabilities of browsers, see comparison of web browsers.
[Contains English characters] Early web browsers supported only a very simple version of HTML.
[Contains English characters] The rapid development of proprietary web browsers led to the development of non-standard dialects of HTML, leading to problems with interoperability.
[Contains English characters] Modern web browsers support a combination of standards-based and de facto HTML and XHTML, which should be rendered in the same way by all browsers.

[Contains English characters] They took good care to secure the fort by a strong garrison, which was well supported with artillery and ammunition.
[Contains English characters] Gingee remained firmly in French possession until after the fall of Pondicherry to Sir Eyre Coote in January 1761. The English commander was Captain Stephen Smith.
[Contains English characters] With the fall of Gingee the French lost their last possession in the Carnatic.
[Contains English characters] Gingee regained its political importance, for the last time in its fateful history, in 1780 A.
[Contains English characters] D, when Haidar Ali, helped by some able French Officers, invaded Carnatic with a force of 90,000 men.
[Contains English characters] Haidar’s men appeared before the fortress and easily carried it by their assault in November 1780. The English re-conquered it at the close of the second Mysore war from Tippu Sultan in 1799. After that Gingee had been free from the ravages and anarchy of war, but subject to desolation and decay.
[Contains English characters] During the frequent Indo-French Wars, the British resident wanted the Fort and The Fortification to be demolished.
[Contains English characters] Luckily his suggestion was not accepted and the Fort remains for us to experience and relive the history.
[Contains English characters] Gingee is located at 12°15′N 79°25′E / 12.25°N 79.42°E / 12.25; 79.42. It has an average elevation of 92 metres .
[Contains English characters] As of 2001 India census, Gingee had a population of 20,896. Males constitute 50% of the population and females 50%.
[Contains English characters] Gingee has an average literacy rate of 73%, higher than the national average of 59.5%: male literacy is 81%, and female literacy is 64%.
[Contains English characters] In Gingee, 11% of the population is under 6 years of age.

[Contains English characters] Master of Commerce is a postgraduate Masters Degree focusing on commerce, management and economics related subjects.
[Contains English characters] Like the undergraduate Bachelor of Commerce, the degree is offered in Commonwealth nations.
[Contains English characters] The Master of Commerce typically requires one year of full-time study.
[Contains English characters] The curriculum is usually concentrated on one subject area — such as accounting, economics, finance or marketing — and emphasises underlying theory.
[Contains English characters] Relatedly, programs usually include a thesis component, or may even be exclusively research based.
[Contains English characters] Given this structure, the MComm differs from other business and management degrees.
[Contains English characters] Its concentration on one area distinguishes it from generalist degrees, such as the मास्टर ऑफ बिझिनेस ऍडमिनीस्ट्रेशन; some universities offer the MComm in general management, although this is more similar to the Master of Management than to the MBA.
[Contains English characters] As compared to specialised Professional degrees - such as the Master of Science in Finance or Master of Accounting - the MComm places more emphasis on theory, although sometimes less on practice; generally, though, there is a close correspondence between these degrees and the related MComm; see also Master of Science in Management.
[Contains English characters] Admission is usually on the basis of an existing Bachelors degree, generally the Bachelor of Commerce.
[Contains English characters] Depending on the degree focus, a related undergraduate major and / or a fairly strong quantitative background may also be a prerequisite.
[Contains English characters] Some programs admit students from non-business backgrounds such as liberal arts, engineering, or the sciences - these programs usually require that students complete a bridging course.
[Contains English characters] Based on specialisation, graduates are typically employed in fields related to their degree focus, such as financial services, marketing and project management; graduates also often work in general management and business consulting .
[Contains English characters] The Master of Commerce includes a research component and thus provides access to a doctorate; progressing from the Master of Commerce, a student can pursue a Doctor of Commerce, Doctor of Business Administration, or a Doctor of Philosophy degree program.

[Contains English characters] It is intended to provide a common source of data which can be used by Wikimedia projects such as Wikipedia, and by anyone else, under a public domain licence.
[Contains English characters] This is similar to the way Wikimedia Commons provides storage for media files and access to those files for all Wikimedia projects, and which are also freely available for reuse.
[Contains English characters] Wikidata is powered by the software Wikibase.
[Contains English characters] Wikidata is a document-oriented database, focused on items.
[Contains English characters] Each item represents a topic and is identified by a unique number, prefixed with the letter Q—for example, the item for the topic Politics is Q7163. This enables the basic information required to identify the topic the item covers to be translated without favouring any language.
[Contains English characters] Information is added to items by creating statements.
[Contains English characters] Statements take the form of key-value pairs, with each statement consisting of a property and a value linked to the property.
[Contains English characters] The creation of the project was funded by donations from the Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence, the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, and Google, Inc.
[Contains English characters] , totaling €1.3 million.
[Contains English characters] Initial development of the project is being overseen by Wikimedia Deutschland and has been split into three phases: Wikidata was launched on 30 October 2012 and was the first new project of the Wikimedia Foundation since 2006. At this time, only the first phase was available.
[Contains English characters] This enabled items to be created and filled with basic information: a label – a name or शीर्षक, aliases – alternative terms for the label, a description, and links to articles about the topic in all the various language editions of Wikipedia.
[Contains English characters] Historically, a Wikipedia article would include a list of interlanguage links, being links to articles on the same topic in other editions of Wikipedia, if present.
[Contains English characters] Initially, Wikidata was a self-contained repository of interlanguage links.
[Contains English characters] No Wikipedia language editions were able to access Wikidata, so they needed to continue to maintain their own lists of interlanguage links.
[Contains English characters] On 14 January 2013, the Hungarian Wikipedia became the first to enable the provision of interlanguage links via Wikidata.
[Contains English characters] This functionality was extended to the Hebrew and Italian Wikipedias on 30 January, to the English Wikipedia on 13 February and to all other Wikipedias on 6 March.
[Contains English characters] After no consensus was reached over a proposal to restrict the removal of language links from the English Wikipedia, the power to delete them from the English Wikipedia was granted to automatic editors .
[Contains English characters] On 23 September 2013, phase 1 went live on Wikimedia Commons.
[Contains English characters] The initial features of the second phase were deployed on 4 February 2013, introducing statements to Wikidata entries.
[Contains English characters] The values were initially limited to two data types, with more data types to follow later.
[Contains English characters] The first new type, string, was deployed on 6 March.
[Contains English characters] The ability for the various language editions of Wikipedia to access data from Wikidata was rolled out progressively between 27 March and 25 April 2013. On 16 September 2015, Wikidata began allowing so-called arbitrary access, or access from a given Wikidata item to the properties of items not directly connected to it.
[Contains English characters] For example, it became possible to read data about Germany from the Berlin article, which was not feasible before.
[Contains English characters] On 27 April 2016 arbitrary access was activated on Wikimedia Commons.
[Contains English characters] Phase 3 will involve database querying and the creation of lists based on data stored on Wikidata.
[Contains English characters] As of October 2016 two tools for querying Wikidata were available: AutoList and PetScan, additionally to a public SPARQL endpoint.
[Contains English characters] There is concern that the project is being influenced by lobbying companies, PR professionals and search engine optimizers.
[Contains English characters] As of December 2015, according to Wikimedia statistics, half of the information in Wikidata is unsourced.
[Contains English characters] Another 30% is labeled as having come from Wikipedia, but with no indication as to which article.
[Contains English characters] The bars on the logo contain the word WIKI encoded in Morse code.

[Contains English characters] More generally, computers can be used to recreate the environment and conditions of the past, such as objects, buildings, landscapes and even ancient battles.

[Contains English characters] As with most academic disciplines, there are a very large number of archaeological sub-disciplines characterised by a specific method or type of material, geographical or chronological focus, other thematic concern, or a specific archaeological culture or civilisation .
[Contains English characters] Historical archaeology is the study of cultures with some form of writing.
[Contains English characters] In इंग्लंड, archaeologists have uncovered the long-lost layouts of medieval villages abandoned after the crises of the 14th century and the equally lost layouts of 17th century parterre gardens swept away by a change in fashion.
[Contains English characters] In downtown New York City archaeologists have exhumed the 18th century remains of the African burial ground.
[Contains English characters] Ethnoarchaeology is the archaeological study of living people.
[Contains English characters] The approach gained notoriety during the emphasis on middle range theory that was a feature of the processual movement of the 1960s.
[Contains English characters] Early ethnoarchaeological research focused on hunting and gathering or foraging societies.
[Contains English characters] Ethnoarchaeology continues to be a vibrant component of post-processual and other current archaeological approaches.
[Contains English characters] Ethnoarchaeology is the use of ethnography to increase and improve analogs, which are then used as analogies to interpret the archaeological record.
[Contains English characters] In short, ethnoarchaeology is the application of ethnography to archaeology.
[Contains English characters] Experimental archaeology represents the application of the experimental method to develop more highly controlled observations of processes that create and impact the archaeological record.
[Contains English characters] In the context of the logical positivism of processualism with its goals of improving the scientific rigor of archaeological epistemologies the experimental method gained importance.
[Contains English characters] Experimental techniques remain a crucial component to improving the inferential frameworks for interpreting the archaeological record.
[Contains English characters] Archaeometry is a field of study that aims to systematize archaeological measurement.
[Contains English characters] It emphasizes the application of analytical techniques from physics, chemistry, and engineering.
[Contains English characters] It is a lively field of research that frequently focuses on the definition of the chemical composition of archaeological remains for source analysis.
[Contains English characters] A relatively nascent subfield is that of archaeological materials, designed to enhance understanding of prehistoric and non-industrial culture through scientific analysis of the structure and properties of materials associated with human activity.
[Contains English characters] साचा:Original research While archaeology can be done as a pure science, it can also be an applied science, namely the study of archaeological sites that are threatened by development.
[Contains English characters] In such cases, archaeology is a subsidiary activity within Cultural resources management, also called heritage management in the United Kingdom.
[Contains English characters] Today, CRM accounts for most of the archaeological research done in the United States and much of that in western Europe as well.
[Contains English characters] In the US, CRM archaeology has been a growing concern since the passage of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966, and most taxpayers, scholars, and politicians believe that CRM has helped preserve much of that nations history and prehistory that would have otherwise been lost in the expansion of cities, dams, and highways.
[Contains English characters] Along with other statutes, the NHPA mandates that projects on federal land or involving federal funds or permits consider the effects of the project on each archaeological site.
[Contains English characters] The application of CRM in the United Kingdom is not limited to government-funded projects.
[Contains English characters] Since 1990 PPG 16 has required planners to consider archaeology as a material consideration in determining applications for new development.
[Contains English characters] As a result, numerous archaeological organisations undertake mitigation work in advance of construction work in archaeologically sensitive areas, at the developers expense.
[Contains English characters] In England, ultimate responsibility of care for the historic environment rests with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport in association with English Heritage.
[Contains English characters] In Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, the same responsibilities lie with Historic Scotland, Cadw and the Northern Ireland Environment Agency respectively.
[Contains English characters] Among the goals of CRM are the identification, preservation, and maintenance of cultural sites on public and private lands, and the removal of culturally valuable materials from areas where they would otherwise be destroyed by human activity, such as proposed construction.
[Contains English characters] This study involves at least a cursory examination to determine whether or not any significant archaeological sites are present in the area affected by the proposed construction.
[Contains English characters] If these do exist, time and money must be allotted for their excavation.
[Contains English characters] If initial survey and/or test excavation indicates the presence of an extraordinarily valuable site, the construction may be prohibited entirely.
[Contains English characters] CRM is a thriving entity, especially in the United States and Europe where archaeologists from private companies and all levels of government engage in the practice of their discipline.
[Contains English characters] Cultural resources management has, however, been criticized.
[Contains English characters] CRM is conducted by private companies that bid for projects by submitting proposals outlining the work to be done and an expected budget.
[Contains English characters] It is not unheard-of for the agency responsible for the construction to simply choose the proposal that asks for the least funding.
[Contains English characters] CRM archaeologists face considerable time pressure, often being forced to complete their work in a fraction of the time that might be allotted for a purely scholarly endeavour.
[Contains English characters] Compounding the time pressure is the vetting process of site reports which are required to be submitted by CRM firms to the appropriate State Historic Preservation Office .
[Contains English characters] From the SHPOs perspective there is to be no difference between a report submitted by a CRM firm operating under a deadline, and a multi-year academic project.
[Contains English characters] The end result is that for a Cultural Resource Management archaeologist to be successful, they must be able to produce academic quality documents at a corporate world pace.
[Contains English characters] The annual ratio of open academic archaeology positions to the annual number of archaeology MA/MSc and PhD students is grossly disproportionate.
[Contains English characters] This dearth of academic positions causes a predictable excess of well educated individuals who join the ranks of the following years crop of non-academically employed archaeologists.
[Contains English characters] Cultural Resource Management, once considered an intellectual backwater for individuals with strong backs and weak minds has reaped the benefit of this massive pool of well educated professionals.
[Contains English characters] This results in CRM offices increasingly staffed by advance degreed individuals with a track record of producing scholarly articles but who have the notches on their trowels to show they have been in the trenches as a shovelbum.
[Contains English characters] Early archaeology was largely an attempt to uncover spectacular artifacts and features, or to explore vast and mysterious abandoned cities.
[Contains English characters] Such pursuits continue to fascinate the public.
[Contains English characters] Books, films, and video games, such as The City of Brass, King Solomons Mines, Indiana Jones, Tomb Raider, The Mummy and Relic Hunter all testify to the publics interest in the discovery aspect of archaeology.
[Contains English characters] Much thorough and productive research has indeed been conducted in dramatic locales such as Copán and the Valley of the Kings, but the bulk of activities and finds of modern archaeology are not so sensational.
[Contains English characters] Archaeological adventure stories tend to ignore the painstaking work involved in carrying out modern survey, excavation, and data processing.
[Contains English characters] Some archaeologists refer to such portrayals as pseudoarchaeology.
[Contains English characters] Archaeology has been portrayed in the mainstream media in sensational ways.
[Contains English characters] This has its advantages and disadvantages.
[Contains English characters] Many practitioners point to the childhood excitement of Indiana Jones films and Tomb Raider video games as the inspiration for them to enter the field.
[Contains English characters] Archaeologists are also very much reliant on public support, the question of exactly who they are doing their work for is often discussed.
[Contains English characters] Motivated by a desire to halt looting, curb pseudoarchaeology, and to help preserve archaeological sites through education and fostering public appreciation for the importance of archaeological heritage, archaeologists are mounting public-outreach campaigns.
[Contains English characters] They seek to stop looting by combatting people who illegally take artifacts from protected sites, and by alerting people who live near archaeological sites of the threat of looting.
[Contains English characters] Common methods of public outreach include press releases, and the encouragement of school field trips to sites under excavation by professional archaeologists.
[Contains English characters] Public appreciation of the significance of archaeology and archaeological sites often leads to improved protection from encroaching development or other threats.
[Contains English characters] One audience for archaeologists work is the public.
[Contains English characters] They increasingly realize that their work can benefit non-academic and non-archaeological audiences, and that they have a responsibility to educate and inform the public about archaeology.
[Contains English characters] Local heritage awareness is aimed at increasing civic and individual pride through projects such as community excavation projects, and better public presentations of archaeological sites and knowledge.
[Contains English characters] The U. S. Dept. of Agriculture, Forest Service operates a volunteer archaeology and historic preservation program called the Passport in Time .
[Contains English characters] Volunteers work with professional USFS archaeologists and historians on national forests throughout the U. S. Volunteers are involved in all aspects of professional archaeology under expert supervision.
[Contains English characters] In the UK, popular archaeology programs such as Time Team and Meet the Ancestors have resulted in a huge upsurge in public interest.
[Contains English characters] Where possible, archaeologists now make more provisions for public involvement and outreach in larger projects than they once did, and many local archaeological organizations operate within the Community archaeology framework to expand public involvement in smaller-scale, more local projects.
[Contains English characters] Archaeological excavation, however, is best undertaken by well-trained staff that can work quickly and accurately.
[Contains English characters] Often this requires observing the necessary health and safety and indemnity insurance issues involved in working on a modern building site with tight deadlines.
[Contains English characters] Certain charities and local government bodies sometimes offer places on research projects either as part of academic work or as a defined community project.
[Contains English characters] There is also a flourishing industry selling places on commercial training excavations and archaeological holiday tours.
[Contains English characters] Archaeologists prize local knowledge and often liaise with local historical and archaeological societies, which is one reason why Community archaeology projects are starting to become more common.
[Contains English characters] Often archaeologists are assisted by the public in the locating of archaeological sites, which professional archaeologists have neither the funding, nor the time to do.
[Contains English characters] Pseudoarchaeology is an umbrella term for all activities that claim to be archaeological but in fact violate commonly accepted and scientific archaeological practices.
[Contains English characters] It includes much fictional archaeological work, as well as some actual activity.
[Contains English characters] Many non-fiction authors have ignored the scientific methods of processual archaeology, or the specific critiques of it contained in post-processualism.
[Contains English characters] An example of this type is the writing of Erich von Däniken.
[Contains English characters] His 1968 book, Chariots of the Gods?
[Contains English characters] , together with many subsequent lesser-known works, expounds a theory of ancient contacts between human civilisation on Earth and more technologically advanced extraterrestrial civilisations.
[Contains English characters] This theory, known as palaeocontact theory, or Ancient astronaut theory, is not exclusively Dänikens, nor did the idea originate with him.
[Contains English characters] Works of this nature are usually marked by the renunciation of well-established theories on the basis of limited evidence and the interpretation of evidence with a preconceived theory in mind.
[Contains English characters] Looting of archaeological sites is an ancient problem.
[Contains English characters] For instance, many of the tombs of the Egyptian pharaohs were looted during antiquity.
[Contains English characters] Archaeology stimulates interest in ancient objects, and people in search of artifacts or treasure cause damage to archaeological sites.
[Contains English characters] The commercial and academic demand for artifacts unfortunately contributes directly to the illicit antiquities trade.
[Contains English characters] Smuggling of antiquities abroad to private collectors has caused great cultural and economic damage in many countries whose governments lack the resources and or the will to deter it.
[Contains English characters] Looters damage and destroy archaeological sites, denying future generations information about their ethnic and cultural heritage.
[Contains English characters] Indigenous peoples especially lose access to and control over their cultural resources, ultimately denying them the opportunity to know their past.
[Contains English characters] Popular consciousness often associates looting with poor Third World countries, but this is a false assumption.
[Contains English characters] A lack of financial resources and political will are chronic worldwide problems inhibiting more effective protection of archaeological sites.
[Contains English characters] Many Native American Indians today, such as Vine Deloria, Jr.
[Contains English characters] , consider any removal of cultural artifacts from a Native American Indian site to be theft, and much of professional archaeology as academic looting.
[Contains English characters] In 1937 W. F. Hodge the Director of the Southwest Museum in Los Angeles CA, released a statement that the museum would no longer purchase or accept collections from looted contexts.
[Contains English characters] The first conviction of the transport of artifacts illegally removed from private property under the Archaeological Resources Protection Act was in 1992 in the State of Indiana.
[Contains English characters] In the United States, examples such as the case of Kennewick Man have illustrated the tensions between Native Americans and archaeologists which can be summarized as a conflict between a need to remain respectful towards burials sacred sites and the academic benefit from studying them.
[Contains English characters] For years, American archaeologists dug on Indian burial grounds and other places considered sacred, removing artifacts and human remains to storage facilities for further study.
[Contains English characters] In some cases human remains were not even thoroughly studied but instead archived rather than reburied.
[Contains English characters] Furthermore, Western archaeologists views of the past often differ from those of tribal peoples.
[Contains English characters] The West views time as linear; for many natives, it is cyclic.
[Contains English characters] From a Western perspective, the past is long-gone; from a native perspective, disturbing the past can have dire consequences in the present.
[Contains English characters] As a consequence of this, American Indians attempted to prevent archaeological excavation of sites inhabited by their ancestors, while American archaeologists believed that the advancement of scientific knowledge was a valid reason to continue their studies.
[Contains English characters] This contradictory situation was addressed by the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, which sought to reach a compromise by limiting the right of research institutions to possess human remains.
[Contains English characters] Due in part to the spirit of postprocessualism, some archaeologists have begun to actively enlist the assistance of indigenous peoples likely to be descended from those under study.
[Contains English characters] Archaeologists have also been obliged to re-examine what constitutes an archaeological site in view of what native peoples believe to constitute sacred space.
[Contains English characters] To many native peoples, natural features such as lakes, mountains or even individual trees have cultural significance.
[Contains English characters] Australian archaeologists especially have explored this issue and attempted to survey these sites in order to give them some protection from being developed.
[Contains English characters] Such work requires close links and trust between archaeologists and the people they are trying to help and at the same time study.
[Contains English characters] While this cooperation presents a new set of challenges and hurdles to fieldwork, it has benefits for all parties involved.
[Contains English characters] Tribal elders cooperating with archaeologists can prevent the excavation of areas of sites that they consider sacred, while the archaeologists gain the elders aid in interpreting their finds.
[Contains English characters] There have also been active efforts to recruit aboriginal peoples directly into the archaeological profession.
[Contains English characters] A new trend in the heated controversy between First Nations groups and scientists is the repatriation of native artifacts to the original descendants.
[Contains English characters] An example of this occurred June 21, 2005, when community members and elders from a number of the 10 Algonquian nations in the Ottawa area convened on the Kitigan Zibi reservation near Maniwaki, Quebec, to inter ancestral human remains and burial goods — some dating back 6,000 years.
[Contains English characters] It was not determined, however, if the remains were directly related to the Algonquin people who now inhabit the region.
[Contains English characters] The remains may be of Iroquoian ancestry, since Iroquoian people inhabited the area before the Algonquin.
[Contains English characters] Alternatively, the oldest of these remains might have no relation at all to the Algonquin or Iroquois, and belong to an earlier culture who previously inhabited the area.
[Contains English characters] The remains and artifacts, including jewelry, tools and weapons, were originally excavated from various sites in the Ottawa Valley, including Morrison and the Allumette Islands.
[Contains English characters] They had been part of the Canadian Museum of Civilization’s research collection for decades, some since the late 1800s.
[Contains English characters] Elders from various Algonquin communities conferred on an appropriate reburial, eventually deciding on traditional redcedar and birchbark boxes lined with redcedar chips, muskrat and beaver pelts.
[Contains English characters] Now, an inconspicuous rock mound marks the reburial site where close to 90 boxes of various sizes are buried, no further scientific study is possible.
[Contains English characters] Although negotiations were at times tense between the Kitigan Zibi community and museum, they were able to reach agreement.
[Contains English characters] Kennewick Man is another repatriation candidate that has been the source of heated debate.

[Contains English characters] It is the oldest film industry in India.
[Contains English characters] The first film in India was a silent film called Raja Harishchandra, which was made in Marathi by a Maharashtrian, Dadasaheb Phalke and a Marathi crew who were performing Marathi & Sanskrit Sangeet natikas and plays in marathi at that period.
[Contains English characters] The first Marathi talkie film, Ayodhyecha Raja was released in 1932, just one year after Alam Ara the first Hindi talkie film.

[Contains English characters] The industry is based in Mumbai, Maharashtra.
[Contains English characters] Marathi Cinema is as old as Indian Cinema.

[Contains English characters] The history of cinema in Bengal dates back to the 1890s, when the first bioscopes were shown in theatres in Calcutta.
[Contains English characters] Within a decade, the first seeds of the industry was sown by Hiralal Sen, considered a stalwart of Victorian era cinema when he set up the Royal Bioscope Company, producing scenes from the stage productions of a number of popular shows at the Star Theatre, Calcutta, Minerva Theatre, Classic Theatre.
[Contains English characters] Following a long gap after Sens works, Dhirendra Nath Ganguly established Indo British Film Co, the first Bengali owned production company, in 1918. However, the first Bengali Feature film, Billwamangal, was produced in 1919, under the banner of Madan Theatre.

[Contains English characters] Besides India, there is a large market for these films in other bhojpuri speaking countries of the West Indies, Oceania, and South America.
[Contains English characters] Bhojpuri language films history begins in 1962 with the well-received film Ganga Maiyya Tohe Piyari Chadhaibo, which was directed by Kundan Kumar.
[Contains English characters] Throughout the following decades, films were produced only in fits and starts.
[Contains English characters] Films such as Bidesiya and Ganga were profitable and popular, but in general Bhojpuri films were not commonly produced in the 1960s and 1970s.
[Contains English characters] The industry experienced a revival in 2001 with the super hit Saiyyan Hamar, which shot the hero of that film, Ravi Kissan, to superstardom.
[Contains English characters] This success was quickly followed by several other remarkably successful films, including Panditji Batai Na Biyah Kab Hoi and Sasura Bada Paisa Wala .
[Contains English characters] In a measure of the Bhojpuri film industrys rise, both of these did much better business in the states of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar than mainstream Bollywood hits at the time, and both films, made on extremely tight budgets, earned back more than ten times their production costs.
[Contains English characters] Although a smaller industry compared to other Indian film industries, the extremely rapid success of their films has led to dramatic increases in Bhojpuri cinemas visibility, and the industry now supports an awards show and a trade magazine, Bhojpuri City.

[Contains English characters] Objectivity is both a central and elusive concept in philosophy.
[Contains English characters] While there is no universally accepted articulation of objectivity, a proposition is generally considered to be objectively true when its truth conditions are mind-independent—that is, not the result of any judgments made by a conscious entity.
[Contains English characters] Objective truths are those which are discovered rather than created.

[Contains English characters] वस्तुनिष्ठ सत्ये आढळतात ते निर्माण करता येत नाहीत In philosophy, an objective fact means a truth that remains true everywhere, independently of human thought or feelings.
[Contains English characters] For instance, it is true always and everywhere that in base 10, 2 plus 2 equals 4.
[Contains English characters] A subjective fact is one that is only true under certain conditions, at certain times, in certain places, or for certain people.
[Contains English characters] Among the truth-conducive tools of thought used by objective thinkers are the scientific virtues.
[Contains English characters] When formulating a hypothesis to explain a particular fact, the explainer makes sure that his or her hypothesis is the simplest one on offer, that it is adequate to all known evidence, that it can predict as diverse an array of phenomena as possible, and that it is fruitfully risky, according to Popperians, but more generally, that it can be verified by new or as yet unperformed experiments or observations.
[Contains English characters] The scientific virtue known as simplicity or parsimony has also come to be known as Ockham’s Razor because of its frequent use by the fourteenth century philosopher William of Ockham, whose primary statement of the principle in his nominalist epistemology is that in accounting for the facts nothing should be assumed as necessary unless it is established through evidentiary experience or reasoning, or is required by the articles of faith.
[Contains English characters] साचा:Original researchObjectivism is a term that describes a branch of philosophy that originated in the early nineteenth century.
[Contains English characters] Gottlob Frege was the first to apply it, when he expounded an epistemological and metaphysical theory contrary to that of Immanuel Kant.
[Contains English characters] Kants rationalism attempted to reconcile the failures he perceived in realism, empiricism, and idealism and to establish a critical method of approach in the distinction between epistemology and metaphysics.
[Contains English characters] Objectivism, in this context, is an alternate name for philosophical realism, the view that there is a reality or ontological realm of objects and facts that exists independent of the mind.
[Contains English characters] Stronger versions of this claim might hold that there is only one correct description of this reality.
[Contains English characters] If it is true that reality is mind-independent, it is thus inclusive of objects that are unknown and not the subject of intentionality.
[Contains English characters] Objectivity in referring requires a definition of truth.
[Contains English characters] According to metaphysical objectivists, an object may truthfully be said to have this or that attribute, as in the statement This object exists, whereas the statement This object is true or false is meaningless.
[Contains English characters] Thus, only propositions have truth values.
[Contains English characters] Essentially, the terms objectivity and objectivism are not synonymous, with objectivism being an ontological theory that incorporates a commitment to the objectivity of objects.
[Contains English characters] Platos realism was a form of metaphysical objectivism, holding that the Ideas exist objectively and independently.
[Contains English characters] Berkeleys empiricist idealism, on the other hand, could be called a subjectivism: he held that things only exist to the extent that they are perceived.
[Contains English characters] Both theories claim methods of objectivity.
[Contains English characters] Platos definition of objectivity can be found in his epistemology, which takes as a model mathematics, and his metaphysics, where knowledge of the ontological status of objects and ideas is resistant to change.
[Contains English characters] Plato considered knowledge of geometry as a condition of philosophical knowledge, both being concerned with universal truths.
[Contains English characters] Platos opposition between objective knowledge and doxa would become the basis for later philosophies intent on resolving the problem of reality, knowledge and human existence.
[Contains English characters] Personal opinions belong to the changing sphere of the sensible, opposed to a fixed and eternal incorporeal realm which is mutually intelligible.
[Contains English characters] Where Plato distinguishes between what and how we know things and their ontological status as things, subjectivism such as Berkeleys and a mind dependence of knowledge and reality fails to make the distinction between what one knows and what is to be known, or in the least explains the distinction superficially.
[Contains English characters] In Platonic terms, a criticism of subjectivism is that it is difficult to distinguish between knowledge, doxa, and subjective knowledge, distinctions which Plato makes.
[Contains English characters] The importance of perception in evaluating and understanding objective reality is debated.
[Contains English characters] Realists argue that perception is key in directly observing objective reality, while instrumentalists hold that perception is not necessarily useful in directly observing objective reality, but is useful in interpreting and predicting reality.
[Contains English characters] The concepts that encompasses these ideas are important in the philosophy of science.
[Contains English characters] The term, ethical subjectivism, covers two distinct theories in ethics.
[Contains English characters] According to cognitive versions of ethical subjectivism, the truth of moral statements depends upon peoples values, attitudes, feelings, or beliefs.
[Contains English characters] Some forms of cognitivist ethical subjectivism can be counted as forms of realism, others are forms of anti-realism.
[Contains English characters] David Hume is a foundational figure for cognitive ethical subjectivism.
[Contains English characters] On a standard interpretation of his theory, a trait of character counts as a moral virtue when it evokes a sentiment of approbation in a sympathetic, informed, and rational human observer.
[Contains English characters] Similarly, Roderick Firths ideal observer theory held that right acts are those that an impartial, rational observer would approve of.
[Contains English characters] William James, another ethical subjectivist, held that an end is good just in case it is desired by that person .
[Contains English characters] According to non-cognitive versions of ethical subjectivism, such as emotivism, prescriptivism, and expressivism, ethical statements cannot be true or false, at all: rather, they are expressions of personal feelings or commands.
[Contains English characters] For example, on A. J. Ayers emotivism, the statement, Murder is wrong is equivalent in meaning to the emotive ejaculation, Murder, Boo!
[Contains English characters] According to the ethical objectivist, the truth or falsity of typical moral judgments does not depend upon the beliefs or feelings of any person or group of persons.
[Contains English characters] This view holds that moral propositions are analogous to propositions about chemistry, biology, or history: they describe a mind-independent reality.
[Contains English characters] When they describe it accurately, they are true --- no matter what anyone believes, hopes, wishes, or feels.
[Contains English characters] When they fail to describe this mind-independent moral reality, they are false --- no matter what anyone believes, hopes, wishes, or feels.
[Contains English characters] There are many versions of ethical objectivism, including various religious views of morality, Platonistic intuitionism, Kantianism, utilitarianism, and certain forms of ethical egoism and contractualism.
[Contains English characters] Note that Platonists define ethical objectivism in an even more narrow way, so that it requires the existence of intrinsic value.
[Contains English characters] Consequently, they reject the idea that contractualists or egoists could be ethical objectivists.

[Contains English characters] Sangam was the ancient academy, which enabled Tamil poets and authors to gather periodically to publish their work.
[Contains English characters] The Sangam met periodically in the city of Madurai in South India under the patronage of the Pandya kings.
[Contains English characters] The current estimate is that the Sangam period lasted between 100 B. C. E. until 300 C.
[Contains English characters] E. The earliest mention of the Sangam is to be found in the 8th century commentary on the Irayanar Agapporul.
[Contains English characters] It mentions three Sangams lasting, at long intervals, for a total of 9990 years.
[Contains English characters] Sangam literature comprises some of the oldest extant Tamil literature, and deals with love, war, governance, trade and bereavement.
[Contains English characters] Unfortunately much of the Tamil literature belonging to the Sangam period had been lost.
[Contains English characters] The literature currently available from this period is perhaps just a fraction of the wealth of material produced during this golden age of Tamil civilisation.
[Contains English characters] In the Sangam literature, the Tamil language had reached a level of maturity and began to serve as a powerful and elegant medium of literary expression.
[Contains English characters] It had already developed an elaborate code of conventions governing the portrayal of social life in literature.
[Contains English characters] This must clearly have been the result of evolution and development spread over some generations.
[Contains English characters] Recent researches examining Chera inscriptions found in southwestern Tamil Nadu have revealed names of three generations of rulers from the Chera clan.
[Contains English characters] These names are also found in some of the Sangam anthology Pathirruppaththu.
[Contains English characters] Palaeographic analysis of the inscriptions has revealed its age to be within the first two centuries of the Common Era.
[Contains English characters] Evidence from ancient Greek and Alexandrian travellers such as Strabo, Ptolemy and Pliny give details of the trade and other relations between the Tamil states and the ancient Greece and Rome.
[Contains English characters] Archaeology has given proof supporting these accounts.
[Contains English characters] Numerous Roman gold and silver coins and pottery have been found from all over Tamil Nadu.
[Contains English characters] It is difficult to estimate the exact date of these Sangam works.
[Contains English characters] The period covered by the extant literature of the Sangam is unfortunately not easy to determine with any measure of certainty.
[Contains English characters] Except the longer epics Cilappatikaram and Manimekalai, which by common consent belong to the age later than the Sangam age, the poems have reached us in the forms of systematic anthologies.
[Contains English characters] Each individual poem has generally attached to it a colophon on the authorship and subject matter of the poem, the name of the king or chieftain to whom the poem relates and the occasion which called forth the eulogy are also found.
[Contains English characters] It is from these colophons and rarely from the texts of the poems themselves, that we gather the names of many kings and chieftains and the poets and poetesses patronised by them.
[Contains English characters] The task of reducing these names to an ordered scheme in which the different generations of contemporaries can be marked off one another has not been easy.
[Contains English characters] To add to the confusions, some historians have even denounced these colophons as later additions and untrustworthy as historical documents.
[Contains English characters] A careful study of the synchronisation between the kings, chieftains and the poets suggested by these colophons indicates that this body of literature reflect occurrences within a period of four or five continuous generations at the most, a period of 120 or 150 years.
[Contains English characters] Any attempt at extracting a systematic chronology and data from these poems should be aware of the casual nature of these poems and the wide difference between the purposes of the anthologist who collected these poems and the historian’s attempts are arriving at a continuous history.
